title: Kinsale Capital's Third-Quarter Combined Ratio Is 75.4% Even as Net Income Falls 31% to $98.1 Million on a $37.6 Million Bond-Sale Loss and Property Premiums Drop 19%
summary: Kinsale Capital reported a third-quarter 2026 combined ratio of 75.4% and underwriting income of $107.1 million, but net income fell to $98.1 million from $141.6 million because of a $37.6 million pre-tax realised loss on a portfolio repositioning, while property premiums fell 19.3% on competition.
description:
Kinsale Capital Group reported third-quarter 2026 results that look contradictory at first glance: a combined ratio of 75.4%, one of the lowest among listed insurers, and net income down by almost a third. The numbers below come from a Reinsurance News report of the company's results. The article does not give earnings per share, book value, buybacks or guidance, so this summary does not cover them. The two halves of the story, strong underwriting and a smaller bottom line, have different causes, and separating them is the key to reading the quarter.

Why net income fell

Third-quarter net income was $98.1 million, compared with $141.6 million in the third quarter of 2025, a drop of about 31%. The report says net income included a $37.6 million pre-tax realised loss from selling fixed-maturity securities, which the company tied to a portfolio repositioning aimed at improving long-term yields. In plain terms, Kinsale sold bonds at a loss, presumably to reinvest in higher-yielding holdings. Such a loss reduces reported profit now in exchange for expected income later, and it does not reflect the cost of claims. The report does not say how much yield the company expects to gain, so the benefit cannot be measured from the article.

For the nine months, net income was $386.6 million, up from $365.0 million. That means the first half of the year was strong enough to leave the year-to-date figure higher than last year even after the weaker third quarter.

Underwriting held up

The underwriting result was steady. Underwriting income was $107.1 million against $105.7 million a year earlier. The combined ratio, which compares claims and expenses with premiums earned, was 75.4% compared with 74.9%. A ratio under 100% means an underwriting profit, so at 75.4% roughly 24.6 cents of every premium dollar earned was left after claims and expenses, a simple calculation from the reported figure. The loss ratio was 53.4% against 53.9%, and the expense ratio was 22.0% against 21.0%. The report says the quarter benefited from higher favourable prior-year reserve development, partly offset by lower ceding commissions resulting from higher treaty retentions. Favourable development means that claims from earlier years turned out cheaper than the company had reserved. Higher retention means Kinsale is passing less risk to reinsurers, which reduces the commissions it receives. The article gives no dollar figure for the reserve release.

Catastrophe losses were small: after-tax catastrophe losses were $1.7 million in the quarter, against $1.0 million a year earlier, and $7.2 million for the nine months, against $21.7 million. The report adds that the 2025 nine-month loss ratio included 2.3 points of net catastrophe losses, mainly from the Palisades Fire in California. Nine-month underwriting income was $307.0 million, up from $268.6 million, and the nine-month combined ratio improved to 76.1% from 77.5%. The nine-month loss ratio was 54.5% against 56.9%, while the expense ratio rose to 21.6% from 20.6%.

Premiums are shrinking in property

The weaker figure is premium growth. Gross written premiums, the total premium written before reinsurance, fell 4.8% to $462.9 million, and nine-month gross written premiums were $1,472.5 million, down 3.5%. Net written premiums fell 1.5% to $399.1 million. Net earned premiums, the revenue recognised in the period, rose 3.0% to $423.5 million, since earned premium lags written premium.

The decline comes from property. Property premiums fell 19.3% in the quarter and 18.7% over nine months, which the report attributes to competition. Commercial property fell 26.8% in the quarter and 29.8% over nine months. Casualty gross written premiums rose 0.9% in the quarter and 3.0% over nine months. This pattern is consistent with a softening property market, in which more insurers compete for the same business and prices fall. Kinsale's response, according to its chief executive, has been to hold its underwriting standards. Michael Kehoe said the quarter's results demonstrate discipline in a competitive market. The statement is the company's own description, but the premium numbers fit it: the company is writing less property business and still earning a very low combined ratio.

Investment income

Net investment income rose 17.5% to $58.3 million. Investment income is the interest and dividends earned on the portfolio, and it has risen as the portfolio has grown and reinvestment yields have been higher. The realised loss on bond sales sits outside this figure, so the two should be read together: income from holdings rose, while the repositioning cost reduced net profit.

What to watch

Three questions follow. First, how far will property premiums fall if competition continues? A 26.8% fall in commercial property premiums in one quarter is large, and the report does not say whether the company expects it to stabilise. Second, will casualty growth speed up? Growth of under 1% in the quarter is slow, and casualty lines are the ones where reserve adequacy is most closely watched by investors. Third, will the repositioned portfolio deliver the higher yield that justified the loss? The answer will appear in later quarters' investment income.

Limits

This article summarises a trade-press report and not the company's full release, so it omits earnings per share, book value and any outlook statements. It is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: Reinsurance News, reporting Kinsale Capital Group results (October 2026)
image_alt: Office buildings representing commercial property insurance (illustrative)
key_points: Third-quarter net income was $98.1 million against $141.6 million a year earlier, a fall of about 31%, after a $37.6 million pre-tax realised loss on selling fixed-maturity securities in a portfolio repositioning aimed at long-term yields.
Underwriting income rose slightly to $107.1 million from $105.7 million, and the combined ratio was 75.4% against 74.9%, with a loss ratio of 53.4% and an expense ratio of 22.0%.
Gross written premiums fell 4.8% to $462.9 million, driven by a 19.3% drop in property premiums that the report attributes to competition, while casualty premiums rose 0.9%.
Net investment income rose 17.5% to $58.3 million, and nine-month underwriting income was $307.0 million against $268.6 million, with a nine-month combined ratio of 76.1%.
Chief executive Michael Kehoe said the quarter's underwriting results demonstrate discipline in a competitive market.
why_it_matters: Kinsale writes hard-to-place commercial risks, so its numbers are a gauge of how pricing competition is affecting specialty insurers. A strong combined ratio alongside shrinking property premiums shows a company choosing margin over volume, while the headline profit drop was caused by an investment decision and not by underwriting.

title: FCA Proposes Scrapping Two General Insurance Value-Measures Reporting Items, Optional for 2026 and 2027 Data and Mandatory From 2028, Ahead of a Wider Review in Early 2027
summary: The Financial Conduct Authority's consultation CP26/33, which closed on 9 October 2026, proposes removing two reporting requirements from its general insurance value measures rules after a post-implementation review found the rules improved transparency but produced inconsistent data, with a wider consultation expected in the first half of 2027.
description:
The Financial Conduct Authority has completed a post-implementation review of the general insurance value measures rules and is consulting on two minor changes to reduce the reporting burden on firms. The consultation, CP26/33, was first published on 11 September 2026, closed on 9 October 2026 and was last updated on 19 October 2026. The details here come from the FCA's own consultation page. The full consultation paper was not reviewed, so details beyond the page's summary are not covered.

What the rules are

The value measures rules were introduced in 2021. They require general insurance firms to report annual data on how their products perform for customers, and the FCA publishes some of this data by firm and product. The measures include claims frequency, claims acceptance rates, average claim pay-outs and the number of claims complaints. The idea is to let anyone compare products on outcomes that matter, such as how often claims are paid and how much is paid out, and not only on price. The rules followed the FCA's 2014 market study on general insurance add-ons and a pilot scheme that ran from 2016 to 2020. Since then the FCA has introduced general insurance pricing practices rules and the Consumer Duty, both of which also shape how firms judge the value of their products.

What the review found

The review concluded that the rules improved transparency and helped firms meet their fair value obligations. It also found that there are reporting inconsistencies which make the data harder to use and compare. That is a significant finding. If two insurers report the same measure in different ways, a comparison between them can mislead, which defeats part of the purpose of publishing the data. The FCA says that a wider consultation on the rules is planned to address these issues.

The two proposed changes

The consultation proposes to remove two reporting requirements:

1. The amount by which the top 2% of claim pay-outs sit above a threshold.
2. The names of a firm's five largest distribution arrangements for each product.

The FCA says it does not publish these data points and does not use them widely in its supervisory work. It argues that removing them will reduce the burden on firms without reducing the usefulness of the data. A distribution arrangement is a relationship through which a product reaches customers, such as a deal with a broker, comparison site or retailer, so the second item would have given the regulator a view of the main channels for each product. The FCA's position is that it can do without it.

Timing

The changes would apply on a transitional, optional basis to data submissions for 2026 and 2027. They would become mandatory from the 2028 reporting year, which would be submitted in 2029. The page states that the changes are expected to take effect from 31 December 2026. In practice, firms would have a choice for two reporting cycles and then no longer need to report the items. The page lists the consultation opening date in a way that looks like a typographical error, and the page metadata gives two publication dates, 8 and 11 September 2026; the 11 September date is used here.

Who is affected

The firms directly affected are general insurance firms that report value measures data, including insurers, intermediaries and managing agents. The page also names trade bodies, consumer organisations, research companies and price comparison websites as groups with an interest, since they use the published data.

Why it is happening now

The consultation sits between two other developments. The first is the Consumer Duty, which requires firms to deliver good outcomes and monitor them. The FCA has also published its views on outcomes monitoring, and value measures data is one input to that. The second is public pressure over insurance outcomes. The FCA's page notes that in 2025 Which? submitted a super-complaint about poor outcomes in home and travel insurance, using value measures data. That shows the data being used by consumer groups to challenge firms, which is one reason the FCA is careful about what it keeps and what it drops.

Next steps

The FCA will publish feedback on the responses and then issue either a policy statement or a handbook notice. It expects to consult on wider changes to value measures in the first half of 2027. The page does not say what those changes will cover. The consultation page does not list the responses it received, and so it is too early to say whether firms or consumer groups supported the proposals.

What it means for firms and consumers

For firms, the likely effect is a modest reduction in reporting work. For consumers and researchers, the data they rely on is unchanged, because the two removed items were not published. The more important event is the wider consultation planned for 2027, which could change the measures themselves and address the inconsistency problem the review identified. Firms that want to influence that review will have an opportunity to respond.

Limits

This article is based on the FCA's consultation web page and not on the consultation paper itself. Proposals may change after consultation. It is general information, not regulatory or legal advice.
image_alt: Documents and a calculator representing regulatory reporting (illustrative)
key_points: CP26/33 proposes removing two items from general insurance value measures reporting: the amount by which the top 2% of claim pay-outs sit above a threshold, and the names of a firm's five largest distribution arrangements for each product.
A post-implementation review found the 2021 rules improved transparency and helped firms meet fair value requirements, but that reporting inconsistencies make the data harder to use and compare.
The changes would be optional for 2026 and 2027 data submissions and mandatory from the 2028 reporting year, which is submitted in 2029.
The FCA says it does not publish the two data points and does not use them widely in supervision, and the consultation closed on 9 October 2026.
A wider consultation on the value measures rules is expected in the first half of 2027.
why_it_matters: Value measures data lets regulators, journalists and consumer groups compare how much insurers pay out on claims and how often they accept them. Trimming the reporting burden while keeping the core measures shows how the FCA is balancing transparency against cost, just before a bigger review of the rules.

title: Lloyd's Sets Conditions for Broker-Originated Reinsurance Structures From January 2027: No Broker Ownership, a 19.99% Managing Agent Stake and a 10% Cap on a Broker's Treaty Portfolio
summary: Lloyd's published Market Bulletin Y5493 on October 16, 2026 setting conditions for broker-originated reinsurance structures from January 1, 2027, including a ban on broker ownership, a minimum managing agent participation of 19.99%, an initial 10% cap on a broker's treaty portfolio and an all-or-nothing cession rule.
description:
Lloyd's of London has set out the conditions under which brokers may route client reinsurance business into capital-backed underwriting vehicles at Lloyd's. The rules were issued in Market Bulletin Y5493 on October 16, 2026 and take effect on January 1, 2027. The details in this article come from an Insurance Business UK report dated October 23, 2026. The bulletin itself was not reviewed, and the report notes that some terms are not publicly defined, so the description below is limited to what the report says.

The background

The bulletin follows months of debate in the market about whether brokers should be allowed to place portfolios of their clients' reinsurance business into vehicles backed by capital market investors. At the Monte Carlo Rendez-Vous in September 2026, reports described a plan by Aon and Blackstone to route part of Aon's brokered reinsurance flow into a Blackstone-backed Lloyd's vehicle. According to the report, neither company has confirmed this publicly, so it is reported speculation and not an announced deal. Lloyd's framed its bulletin as conditions for operating, not a ban, which the report reads as a sign that Lloyd's sees legitimate demand for such structures.

The central concern is one of roles. A broker acts for the client who buys reinsurance, while an underwriter takes risk. If a broker also has a financial interest in the vehicle that takes the risk, the broker's advice to clients may be influenced by its own interest. The conditions are designed to limit that overlap.

The main requirements

Broker ownership. Brokers cannot own or capitalise these structures. The report says this addresses concerns that such arrangements blur the line between intermediary and underwriter.

Managing agent capital. The managing agent, the firm that runs a syndicate at Lloyd's, must hold a minimum participation of 19.99%. The report notes that this sits just below the 20% level at which Lloyd's and FCA rules treat a holder as having significant influence, which triggers additional approval. The aim is for the managing agent to have real exposure to the book it underwrites.

Concentration cap. Initially, no more than 10% of an individual broker's treaty portfolio may be placed into these structures. Lloyd's describes this as an initial appetite and may revise it. A treaty portfolio is a broker's book of treaty reinsurance placements, so the cap limits how much of a broker's business can flow into a single type of vehicle.

All-or-nothing cession. A cedant, the insurer buying reinsurance, must cede either all of its eligible portfolio with the broker to the structure or none of it. The report says this prevents cedants from moving only their better business and leaving weaker risks elsewhere, a practice sometimes called cherry-picking.

Obligations on managing agents and brokers

Managing agents must show strong reinsurance pricing skills, portfolio solutions expertise, and sufficient access to data to validate and challenge the broker's assumptions. Brokers must provide monthly data to the managing agents, including dashboards, exception reports and bind-level data, and must report quarterly to Lloyd's. Annual plans and mid-year changes need approval from the Lloyd's Corporation Performance Group.

Cedants must share in the operational and capital efficiencies the structure produces. The report calls this one of the framework's more direct consumer-protection measures, and says that its adequacy will depend on how those efficiencies are priced against running costs.

Exclusions and conditions

Certain business types are excluded: hybrid fronting carriers, managing general underwriters and legacy providers. Involvement of captives requires a prior submit arrangement, and structures cannot carry exposure to cyber war "type 4" language. The report does not define these terms further.

The performance backstop

If a structure has not reached at least 70% indexation by year three, Lloyd's and the managing agent must agree next steps, which may include winding up. The report notes that Lloyd's has not publicly defined the indexation metric in the summaries available. It advises prospective participants to seek clarification through the new entrant process before January 1, 2027. The framework runs alongside the existing new entrant approval process and ongoing oversight.

What to watch

Four points will matter in practice. First, whether any broker-backed vehicle applies under the new framework before the January start date. Second, whether the 10% cap is raised once Lloyd's has seen how the structures behave. Third, how the client dividend requirement is priced, since it determines whether clients gain anything. Fourth, how the 70% indexation test is defined, because it determines when a structure could be wound up.

Who is affected

The framework matters most to three groups. Brokers that have been considering such vehicles now know the limits on ownership and volume. Managing agents, which would run the underwriting, must decide whether a 19.99% participation and the data obligations are worth taking on. And cedants, the insurers buying reinsurance, are told they can expect to share in any efficiencies, but only if they commit their whole eligible portfolio with the broker. One practical point follows from the rules as reported: a cedant must commit everything before it knows how large its share of the efficiencies will be, because that depends on how the dividend is priced.

Limits

This article relies on a single trade report of the bulletin and does not reproduce the bulletin's text. The Aon and Blackstone plan is unconfirmed, and nothing in the report indicates that either company has applied to Lloyd's. It is general information, not legal or investment advice.
source_name: Insurance Business UK, reporting Lloyd's Market Bulletin Y5493 (October 23, 2026)
image_alt: City skyline representing the London insurance market (illustrative)
key_points: Lloyd's Market Bulletin Y5493, published on October 16, 2026, sets a framework that takes effect on January 1, 2027 for broker-originated reinsurance structures seeking approval to operate at Lloyd's.

Brokers cannot own or capitalise the structures, and the managing agent must hold a minimum participation of 19.99%, just under the 20% level at which Lloyd's and FCA rules treat a holder as having significant influence.
Initially no more than 10% of an individual broker's treaty portfolio may be placed into these structures, and cedants must cede either all of their eligible portfolio with the broker or none of it.
Brokers must provide monthly data to managing agents and report quarterly to Lloyd's, and cedants must share in the operational and capital efficiencies.
If a structure has not reached at least 70% indexation by year three, Lloyd's and the managing agent must agree next steps, which may include winding up.
why_it_matters: Brokers sit between clients and insurers, and a structure that routes a broker's reinsurance placements into a capital-backed vehicle raises conflict-of-interest questions. Lloyd's rules show how the market's gatekeeper wants such vehicles to operate, and they affect brokers, managing agents and the investors behind them.

title: Federal Court Finds Two Former Youpla Group Leaders Breached Their Duties Over a Related-Party Insurer, With a A$250,000 Penalty and 15-Year Ban Agreed for One Director
summary: ASIC announced on October 30, 2026 that the Federal Court of Australia has found two former directors and officers of the collapsed Youpla Group breached their duties, with Ronald Pattenden agreeing to a A$250,000 penalty and a 15-year ban, while penalties for Bryn Jones and decisions on three others remain outstanding.
description:
The Federal Court of Australia has found that two former leaders of the collapsed Youpla Group breached their duties as company officers, in a case brought by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission over the group's use of a related-party insurer. ASIC announced the findings on October 30, 2026, and Insurance Business Australia reported them on October 31. The details below come from that report; the court judgment itself was not reviewed. Some of the underlying facts are described in the report as ASIC's allegations, and this article keeps that distinction.

Who was sued, and what was found

ASIC sued five former Youpla Group directors and officers in August 2023. They are Bryn Jones, the former chief executive, Ronald Pattenden, a director, and Jonathan Law, Michael Wilson and Geoffrey Clayton. The court has so far found that Pattenden breached his duties as a director of Youpla Group companies. He agreed a joint proposal with ASIC for a penalty of A$250,000 and a 15-year ban from managing corporations. A ban from managing corporations prevents a person from acting as a director or taking part in management of a company.

Jones was also found to have breached his duties, after a contested liability hearing in February. His penalties will be decided at a separate hearing, and the report says the date is still to be scheduled. Decisions on Law, Wilson and Clayton are reserved, meaning the court has not yet announced its findings on them.

The related-party insurer

The insurer at the centre of the case was Crown Insurance Services, a company based in Vanuatu. According to the report, Pattenden and Law beneficially owned and controlled it. ASIC alleged that from September 2017 to November 2018 the directors and officers kept Youpla's insurance arrangements with Crown, and that those arrangements were not in the interests of the fund and benefited Pattenden and Law. ASIC also alleged that the arrangements left the funds exposed to unaffordable premium increases, which took effect in September 2017, and that members continued to pay premiums without knowing the risk to the funds' viability. The report presents these points as ASIC's allegations. It does not say which of them the court accepted in each person's case, so readers should not assume that every allegation was proved.

The people affected

The fund entities were formerly the Aboriginal Community Benefit Fund, known as ACBF, a funeral insurer whose members were largely First Nations families. Funeral cover of this kind is bought in advance so that a family can pay for a funeral when a member dies, and members typically pay premiums over many years. The entities went into liquidation in March 2022, and SV Partners is managing the liquidation. In 2025, the Federal Court ordered ACBF to pay A$3.5 million for misrepresenting that it was Aboriginal owned or managed. In 2024, the government set up the Youpla Support Program in response to the collapse. The report says applications to that program closed on June 30, and payments will be processed until December 1.

What ASIC said

ASIC chair Sarah Court said the regulator had taken decisive action to ensure those responsible for serious governance failures are held to account, and that the breaches went to the heart of trust and responsibility in the First Nations community. These are quotations from the ASIC statement as reported, in part.

The lesson for boards and brokers

The report draws out a point for brokers who place directors and officers liability cover or advise boards: the case puts on the court record a conflict that is easy to describe and hard to manage, in which the people who chose an entity's insurer also owned that insurer. In general terms, when a company buys insurance from a business connected to its directors, the directors must be able to show that the choice served the company and its members and not themselves. The report does not describe what controls the group had in place, and the findings so far concern specific individuals.

What remains open

Three things are still to come. Jones's penalty hearing has not been scheduled. The decisions on Law, Wilson and Clayton remain outstanding. And the report does not say whether the agreed penalty for Pattenden has been formally approved by the court, only that he agreed to a joint proposal with ASIC. Anyone affected should check ASIC's announcement and the court's orders for the final outcome.

How the pieces fit together

Reading the report as a timeline helps. The group's insurance arrangements with Crown, as ASIC alleged them, ran from September 2017 to November 2018. ASIC sued in August 2023. The fund entities had already gone into liquidation in March 2022. A contested liability hearing for Jones took place in February, and the findings were announced in October 2026. From the alleged conduct to the announced findings is therefore about eight years, a reminder of how long corporate misconduct cases can take, and of how long affected families wait. The government's support program, set up in 2024, was a separate response to the collapse and does not depend on the court outcome.

Limits

This article is based on a single trade-press report of an ASIC announcement. It does not reproduce the judgment, and statements described as allegations have not been treated as proven. It is general information, not legal advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia, reporting ASIC's announcement (October 31, 2026)
image_alt: Gavel and legal documents representing a court judgment (illustrative)
key_points: ASIC announced on October 30, 2026 that the Federal Court found former Youpla Group director Ronald Pattenden and former chief executive Bryn Jones breached their duties; the case was filed in August 2023 against five former directors and officers.
Pattenden agreed a joint proposal with ASIC for a A$250,000 penalty and a 15-year ban from managing corporations; Jones's penalty will be decided at a separate hearing.
Decisions on Jonathan Law, Michael Wilson and Geoffrey Clayton are reserved.

ASIC alleged that from September 2017 to November 2018 the group kept insurance arrangements with Crown Insurance Services, a Vanuatu-based company beneficially owned and controlled by Pattenden and Law, and that this was not in the funds' interests.
The fund entities, formerly the Aboriginal Community Benefit Fund, a funeral insurer whose members were largely First Nations families, went into liquidation in March 2022.
why_it_matters: The people who chose an insurer for a funeral fund also owned that insurer, according to ASIC's allegations. The court's findings put a conflict of interest on the record in a case that affected First Nations families who paid for funeral cover, and they show how directors' duties apply when a related party profits from the fund's insurance.

title: NSW Regulator Penalises NRMA Insurance A$479,500 Over Eight CTP Pricing Failures, Led by an Address-Data Error That Overcharged More Than 41,000 Policyholders About A$12.2 Million
summary: The New South Wales State Insurance Regulatory Authority imposed A$479,500 in civil penalties on Insurance Australia Limited, trading as NRMA Insurance, on October 22, 2026 for eight CTP premium pricing failures, the largest of which affected about 41,564 policies with estimated gross overcharges of about A$12.2 million.
description:
The New South Wales State Insurance Regulatory Authority, known as SIRA, has imposed A$479,500 in civil penalties on Insurance Australia Limited, which trades as NRMA Insurance, over eight separate premium pricing failures in its compulsory third party (CTP) insurance book. SIRA issued the penalties on October 22, 2026, and Insurance Business Australia reported the decision on October 28. The details in this article come from that report. The article does not mention a court, and the decision document itself was not reviewed.

How the penalty was set

The total of A$479,500 already includes a 15% discount on the combined figure. SIRA applied the discount because several of the errors shared a root cause in the HUON operating environment and reflected broader control weaknesses. That is, the regulator treated them as related, not as eight unconnected mistakes. The report also gives a history. In December 2024, SIRA imposed a A$10,000 penalty on NRMA Insurance for failures to apply demerit-point loadings correctly, which affected tens of thousands of CTP policies. The report says the later penalty bill is nearly 48 times larger. On March 31, 2026, special licence conditions were placed on NRMA's CTP licence.

NRMA argued that a formal warning would be more appropriate, citing its cooperation, its corrective action and the licence conditions. SIRA gave weight to its remediation but found that penalties were warranted because of the seriousness of the failures, the impact on customers and the CTP scheme, the control breakdowns and the need for deterrence.

The eight matters

1. The HUON address-data error, described as the most serious. An address-data misconfiguration caused the wrong rating districts to be applied. About 41,564 policies were affected, with estimated gross overcharges of about A$12,175,687, or roughly A$12.2 million, across more than 41,000 policyholders. Simple arithmetic on those two figures gives an average of about A$293 per affected policy, a calculation made here and not stated in the report.

2. A missed discount. For 19 months, from April 2024 to November 2025, NRMA did not apply a discount that it had filed with the regulator to eligible new customers. About 16,033 policies were affected, with estimated overcharges of about A$662,000.

3. Vehicle-risk weightings. Incorrect weightings were uploaded to the pricing system, touching about 303,475 policies. Most of the financial gap was undercharging, of about A$1.7 million, which NRMA did not seek to recover from customers.

4. Loyalty-tenure data. From April 2024, inaccurate loyalty-tenure information appeared in CTP renewal documents and was used to calculate renewal discounts. About 727,000 policies need data review and about 611,000 customers need assessment. The report stresses that these are review populations and not confirmed affected populations, and that SIRA said the penalty was not based on any assumed customer loss.

5. Cancellation refunds. Refunds were calculated from the wrong date, short-changing about 15,176 policyholders by an estimated A$118,421.

6. Risk-state mapping. Incorrect mapping affected 2,831 policies.

7. The pricing cap. A wrong input to the malus factor, the element that sets the maximum premium, pushed premiums above the regulatory ceiling for about 24,579 policies over 19 days in early 2026.

8. An outdated premium filing. For 12 days in January 2025, NRMA used an outdated premium filing, which resulted in an under-collection of A$81,568 in statutory levies.

The breadth of the list shows that the problems were not confined to one rating factor. They involved address data, discounts, weightings, refunds, mapping, a cap and a filing. SIRA's decision to treat them together under a discount reflects its finding of a common control weakness.

What happens next

The penalties do not end NRMA's obligations. It must finish outstanding customer remediation, comply with the special licence conditions and meet other regulatory requirements. The decision states that further non-compliance may lead to further regulatory action. The report does not detail the remediation timeline, and it does not give the number of contraventions beyond the eight matters.

What it means for drivers and insurers

For drivers, the practical point is that CTP premiums in New South Wales are calculated from filed rates and regulated rules, and that errors in the inputs can lead to overcharges. The report does not say how customers will be repaid or contacted, so affected drivers should look for direct communication from NRMA. For insurers, the decision shows that data governance in pricing systems is a regulatory issue, not only an operational one, and that regulators may escalate penalties when similar failures recur.

Scale in context

The eight matters touch very different numbers of policies. The largest by reach is the vehicle-risk weighting error, which touched about 303,475 policies, and the loyalty-tenure review populations of about 727,000 policies are larger still. But the money involved is not proportional to the number of policies. The address-data error affected about 41,564 policies and produced overcharges of about A$12.2 million, whereas the vehicle-risk weightings involved a larger number of policies and most of the financial gap ran in customers' favour, as undercharging of about A$1.7 million that NRMA did not seek to recover. The pattern shows why SIRA looked at the seriousness and control breakdowns and not only at the dollar totals, and why it said the penalty for the loyalty-tenure matter was not based on any assumed customer loss.

Limits

This article is based on a single trade-press report and not on SIRA's decision. Figures are estimates as reported. It is general information, not legal advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia, reporting SIRA's decision (October 28, 2026)
image_alt: Cars on a road representing compulsory third party motor insurance (illustrative)
key_points: SIRA imposed A$479,500 in civil penalties on October 22, 2026 for eight separate CTP premium pricing failures, with a 15% discount applied because several errors shared a root cause in the HUON operating environment.
The most serious failure was an address-data misconfiguration that applied incorrect rating districts to about 41,564 policies, with estimated gross overcharges of about A$12,175,687.

Other failures included a discount filed with the regulator that was not applied for 19 months to about 16,033 policies, and a pricing-cap input error that pushed premiums above the regulatory ceiling for about 24,579 policies over 19 days.
The report says the penalty is nearly 48 times larger than the A$10,000 penalty SIRA imposed in December 2024, and special licence conditions were placed on NRMA's CTP licence on March 31, 2026.
SIRA said the penalties do not end NRMA's obligations to finish customer remediation, and further non-compliance may lead to further action.
why_it_matters: Compulsory third party premiums are filed with and regulated by the state, so errors in how they are calculated can affect tens of thousands of drivers at once. The decision shows how a regulator treats repeated pricing control failures, and how much weight it gives to remediation compared with deterrence.

title: Australia's Declared-Event Home Claims Reach A$11.3 Billion Since 2022 With Queensland Accounting for More Than Half of Claims, as Insurers Urge a Tougher Planning Policy
summary: Insurers received more than 400,000 home repair and rebuild claims from declared events in Australia from 2022 to 2026 at an insured cost of A$11.3 billion, with Queensland accounting for over 214,000 claims, as the Insurance Council of Australia urges that natural hazard protections stay central to Queensland's State Planning Policy review.
description:
Australian insurers have produced an insured cost of A$11.3 billion on home repair and rebuild claims from declared disaster events since 2022, and the state that has generated most of the claims is now reviewing the planning rules that decide where homes are built. The figures come from an Insurance Business Australia report published on October 27, 2026. The headline figure is national, not for Queensland alone, and the report does not explicitly attribute it to a named source, although it appears alongside the Insurance Council of Australia's submission. That limitation is worth keeping in mind.

The claims numbers

For declared events from 2022 to 2026, insurers received more than 400,000 claims nationally to repair or rebuild homes, at an insured cost of A$11.3 billion. Queensland had over 214,000 claims, almost double New South Wales, which had 116,000, while Victoria had 25,000. The report concludes that Queensland has absorbed more than half of national disaster claims over the past four years. The data are measured in claim numbers for Queensland and not in dollars, so the state's share of the A$11.3 billion cannot be calculated from the article.

The report also gives a comparison drawn from the ICA submission: in 2025, declared events damaged 145,392 homes nationally, while 172,657 new homes were completed that year. In other words, the number of homes damaged was equal to about 84% of the number built, a ratio calculated here from those two figures. The comparison illustrates why insurers argue that housing supply and disaster resilience are linked.

The planning review

The Insurance Council of Australia made a submission to the review of Queensland's State Planning Policy. The government is simplifying the framework and standardising flood mapping, and the ICA asked that natural hazard protections remain central to planning decisions. According to the report, its requests include:

- Consistent planning and building rules across all councils, calibrated to each area's hazard risk.
- Safeguards so that simplified rules do not weaken standards, including for infill housing in established suburbs.
- Explicit recognition of climate change, with planning for projected impacts out to 2075 to 2100, aligned with Victoria's flood guidelines.
- Coverage of all extreme weather. The ICA says cyclones and storms appear absent from the current draft, which refers to floods, bushfires and coastal erosion.
- A clear definition of acceptable and tolerable risk.
- Council decisions backed by an evidence base, with state oversight.
- Consistent, up-to-date flood mapping, with data accessible to homeowners, insurers, councils and government agencies.

The ICA is developing a national Climate Risk Land Use Planning Framework with the Planning Institute of Australia. The report notes that Victoria recently gazetted mandatory flood planning rules using a five-tier Flood Risk Rating system that restricts development in the highest-risk zones, and that the ICA suggests Queensland pursue similar consistency. The ICA estimates that around 1.36 million properties nationally are in flood-risk areas. In Logan, updated council flood maps prompted debate among property owners about whether the new risk ratings were accurate, given their pricing implications.

Rebuild costs

The report cites Cotality's Cordell Construction Cost Index, as quoted in the ICA submission, saying a standard Queensland home costs about 45% more to build than in 2021. It adds that Queensland has a projected A$127.5 billion in planned engineering construction over five years, driven largely by the Brisbane 2032 Olympics, according to the Queensland Major Contractors Association. Higher rebuild costs raise claim sizes, and competing demand for builders can slow repairs.

Affordability and funding

The report cites the ACCC's fifth insurance monitoring report from June 2026: the Cyclone Reinsurance Pool cut home insurance premiums by 14% in higher cyclone-risk areas, while average premiums elsewhere rose 10% to A$2,310 between 2023-24 and 2024-25. Average home and contents premiums exceed A$3,100 in north Queensland. In October 2026, all 77 Queensland mayors signed an open letter to the Prime Minister opposing proposed changes to the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements that would move the Commonwealth share from about 64% to a 50-50 split. They warned this could raise premiums and strain council budgets.

What the insurers are saying

ICA deputy chief executive Kylie Macfarlane argued that location decisions affect long-term exposure to floods, cyclones and bushfires, that getting location right supports housing supply as well as safety, and that risk reduction over time brings premiums down. The report adds practical advice for brokers: check that flood and hazard data used at renewal matches the insurer's data, discuss flood cover with clients who lack it, and review sums insured against current replacement values.

What is not in the report

The report contains no response from the Queensland government to the ICA submission or to the mayors' letter, so the outcome of the review is unknown. It is also not clear how much of the A$11.3 billion has been paid, as opposed to estimated, because the report refers to insured cost.

Limits

This article is based on one trade-press report and the submission it describes. The ICA is an industry body with an interest in the outcome. It is general information, not insurance advice.

key_points: From 2022 to 2026, declared events produced more than 400,000 national claims to repair or rebuild homes at an insured cost of A$11.3 billion; the figure is a national total, not a Queensland figure.
Queensland had over 214,000 of those claims, almost double New South Wales' 116,000, with Victoria on 25,000, so Queensland absorbed more than half of national disaster claims over four years.

The Insurance Council of Australia asked that natural hazard protections stay central to Queensland's State Planning Policy review, including consistent rules, flood mapping and explicit recognition of climate change out to 2075 to 2100.
A standard Queensland home costs about 45% more to build than in 2021, according to Cotality's Cordell Construction Cost Index as cited in the ICA submission.

The ACCC's June 2026 report found the Cyclone Reinsurance Pool cut premiums by 14% in higher cyclone-risk areas, and all 77 Queensland mayors opposed proposed changes to disaster recovery funding arrangements.
why_it_matters: Where homes are built determines how much they cost to insure for decades. With Queensland generating more than half of the nation's disaster claims, the planning rules now under review will shape insurance affordability, and the insurers' submission shows what they want those rules to include.
